Capitalism uses prices to decide what should be produced, socialism basically uses feelings. The former works via revealed preferences (what you're willing to pay for, and how hard you're willing to work for it) and the latter via stated preferences (what you claim to want, regardless of the effort you're personally willing to go to to make it a reality).

The problem with socialism is that if the offered effort doesn't match the demanded goods then there is an imbalance that can temporarily be overcome with force (democratic socialism) but eventually will crash the economy. Obviously Libertarian Socialism can't use force to remedy this, so it must have a way of allowing everyone to state what they want, and what they're prepared to do to achieve it, but not via a democratic process where the majority can force their will on the minority.

So here's the difference: Instead of one person advertising "haircuts $5" and another advertising "lunchtime special: $10" (as per normal libertarianism), there would be a big meeting where everyone says what they can offer, and they change their offer based on what everyone else is offering, until nobody wants to change their offer any more. Then they all go off to do what they agreed to do, and it ends up with the hairdresser being able to have a lunchtime special for every 2 haircuts they perform.

It's not that simple though, because this is a static model. In real life the hairdresser might injure her hand and not be able to fulfil her obligation to the society, or a miner might find that their underground reserves are less than they expected. They would have to call a halt to everyone's work, draw a line under the previous economic plan, and have another meeting so a new matrix of production and consumption decisions can be agreed on.

In the silicon age there would be an ebay-like solution to this where people could continually hold such meetings and agree new economic plans as any unforseen circumstance arises. But it couldn't be a solution that involved a price structure, because that would be plain old libertarianism.
